clinical_targets.goal: ≥ 50% reduction in monthly attack/seizure frequency from baseline
Preservation of modified Rankin Scale score ≤ 2
Maintenance of baseline MoCA / MMSE cognitive scores

steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
Step 3: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
Step 4: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Chronic Pain focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.role: Standard initial therapy for mild-to-moderate Chronic Pain.
drug_classes.dosing: Initiate standard therapeutic dosing; titrate over 2–4 weeks based on clinical response and tolerability.
drug_classes.pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Adjunctive or alternative therapy for treatment escalation in Chronic Pain.
drug_classes.dosing: Introduce second-line agent as add-on dual therapy or sequential switch; reassess at 4–6 weeks.
drug_classes.pearls: Screen for drug-drug interactions and additive adverse effects before combining systemic agents.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Chronic Pain require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Chronic Pain.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.
Screen for drug-drug interactions and additive adverse effects before combining systemic agents.
Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.
Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Gabapentinoids, levetiracetam, and topiramate require strict renal dose adjustments.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Valproate, carbamazepine, and phenytoin are extensively metabolized by the liver; monitor serum levels.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Valproate is strictly contraindicated due to high neural tube and neurodevelopmental teratogenicity.
special_populations.elderly: Increased sensitivity to CNS sedatives, anticholinergics, and antiepileptic neurotoxicity; start low and titrate slowly.

style_3_monograph.summary: What is chronic pain? Pain is a signal from your nervous system that something may be wrong. It is an unpleasant feeling, such as a prick, tingle, sting, burn, or ache. Pain may be sharp or dull. You may feel pain in one area of your body or all over. Each person feels pain differently, even if the reason for the pain is the same. Pain might be acute or chronic. The type of pain is based on how long and how often you have pain. Acute pain starts suddenly and goes away when the cause is treated or healed. This pain lets you know that you may be injured or have a problem you need to take care of. Chronic pain lasts longer than three months or the time in which you should have healed. If you have chronic pain, it can occur most days or every day and may last for weeks, months, or even years. It can affect all aspects of daily life, including your mood and relationships. Treatment may not get rid of chronic pain, but it can help with your symptoms. What causes chronic pain? Sometimes, acute pain can become chronic pain. The original cause may have been an injury or infection, or you may have an ongoing cause of pain, such as arthritis or cancer . In some cases, there is no clear cause. Environmental factors and psychological factors such as mood and stress can make chronic pain worse. What are the symptoms of chronic pain? Since people feel pain in different ways, two people could have the same issue, but each may have different symptoms. Chronic pain can occur anywhere in your body and may cause other symptoms such as fatigue , mood changes, or difficulty sleeping . If you have depression or stress, it may make chronic pain worse. Who is more likely to get chronic pain? Many older adults have chronic pain. Women also report having more chronic pain than men, and they are at a greater risk for many pain conditions. Some people have two or more chronic pain conditions. You may be more likely to have chronic pain if you have certain medical conditions such as: Headaches or migraines Cancer Fibromyalgia Arthritis Nerve damage Back problems How is chronic pain diagnosed? Chronic pain lasts three months or longer or when pain continues after your body has healed. If the cause of your pain is unknown, your health care provider may: Ask you about your medical history Ask you to describe the pain and how it affects your life Do a physical exam Order blood tests or other medical tests What are the treatments for chronic pain? Chronic pain is not always curable, but treatments can help. Treatments may include medicines, including pain relievers . There are also non-drug treatments , such as acupuncture , physical therapy, and sometimes surgery. Depending on the cause of your pain and your symptoms, your provider may also recommend lifestyle changes which may include suggestions for: Improving mental health Managing stress Getting to and staying at a healthy weight Adding low-impact exercise
